panel.name: Clostridioides difficile
panel.reason: the clinical endpoint: secondary C. difficile infection is what collateral damage to the gut actually costs. 2,471 MIC records in ChEMBL 37

panel.name: Enterococcus faecalis
panel.reason: Gram-positive pathogen arm; grows either way, so it also serves as the aerobic control for the plate

panel.name: Bacteroides fragilis
panel.reason: best-covered gut anaerobe in ChEMBL (1,000 MIC records) and genuinely both commensal and pathogen, so it sets the ambiguous middle of the window

panel.name: Bifidobacterium longum
panel.reason: the commensal to spare; 243 MIC records, the most of any true gut commensal

controls: reference antibiotic at an inhibitory concentration

rationale: The question is not what this compound's MIC is but whether there is a dose window that clears the pathogens while leaving the commensals above their MIC, so the measurement is a ratio: lowest pathogen MIC against highest commensal MIC. A top of 256 ug/mL over 10 two-fold steps reaches 0.5, which brackets both arms on one plate - commensal MICs in the literature are mostly right-censored at >128, and a typical pathogen MIC is 0.5-4. Every row of a plate shares the same series because the 8-channel pipette carries a whole column, so one ladder has to cover both. 256 rather than 200 keeps every rung on the doubling ladder MICs are reported on. Caveat the plate cannot resolve: above ~128 ug/mL many compounds precipitate, and an OD590 read cannot distinguish compound turbidity from growth - which would make a compound look like it failed to spare a commensal when it merely fell out of solution.
